task: Give the weakest target-language landmark buildings a distinct, recognisable identity in the 3D ESL town-builder. These are the buildings the lesson names out loud ('We have a bakery in Matsubara'), so a child must be able to tell which one is which at a glance.
notes: PROJECT: Vite + three.js, no framework. A 3D town an elementary-school class builds by speaking English. Art direction is 'toy town': chunky low-poly shapes, flat cheerful colours, MeshLambertMaterial under a hemisphere + directional light. Preserve that exactly - this is about charm and legibility within the style, not realism, not textures.

WHY THIS MATTERS PEDAGOGICALLY: the child says the building's name in English and it appears. If the bakery, the cafe and the bookstore are the same box with a different word on the sign, the vocabulary has no visual hook. Each target building should be identifiable from its shape and props even with the sign hidden.

WHERE THE WEAKNESS IS: src/config/landmarks.js maps each landmark type to either a bespoke `factory` or a generic `fallback`. The bespoke ones (school, hospital, library, station, and the other original hand-built landmarks in src/buildings/procedural.js) are already good - LEAVE THOSE ALONE. The weak ones are the landmarks falling through to the generic `shopFront()` and `civicBlock()` builders in src/buildings/extras.js, which produce essentially one box with an awning and a sign board. Read landmarks.js first and list which types actually use the generic builders - those are your scope.

PICK THE HIGH-VALUE ONES. Do not attempt every landmark. Choose roughly six to eight of the generic-built target words that a Japanese elementary class would actually practise - typical candidates are bakery, cafe, restaurant, bookstore, convenience store, post office, bank, gym, hotel - and give each a bespoke silhouette and one or two signature props. A bakery might get an awning, a bread-shaped sign and window trays; a post office a red pillar box and a service counter window; a gym a tall clerestory windowed hall. Use your judgement about which read best; say in your report which you did and which you left generic.

SHARED LANGUAGE ALREADY EXISTS - use it. src/world/props.js exports addBuildingPlinth() and addPitchedRoofFinish(), and the ambient houses/shops were recently given four-sided detail, ground contact and roofline articulation. New landmark work should sit in that same visual family. See DESIGN_DECISIONS.md, '2026-09-06 - Procedural buildings use a four-sided toy-town kit'.

PERFORMANCE IS A HARD CONSTRAINT: Japanese elementary-school Chromebooks with integrated GPUs. src/core/materials.js caches every material and geometry so the renderer can batch. Reuse mat()/box()/roundedBox()/cylinder()/sphere() from that module; no per-instance materials, no MeshStandardMaterial, no new lights, no per-frame work.

SIZE DISCIPLINE: each landmark is built into a lot with a fixed envelope. A building that outgrows its plot ends up standing on the public sidewalk, which was a real bug here before. .ai/audit-landmark-extents.mjs measures every landmark against its lot - run it and do not introduce a new spill. (The 'station' row reports a huge width because it includes the railway track; that is a known pre-existing artifact of the audit, not a regression - ignore that one row.)
Record what you changed and why in DESIGN_DECISIONS.md and update CURRENT_STATE.md.
requirements: Roughly six to eight generic-built target-language landmarks each gain a distinct silhouette and signature props, so they are tellable apart without reading the sign.
Each reworked building looks finished from all four sides - the camera orbits freely.
Each sits on the ground properly (plinth/approach) and has articulated roof edges, consistent with the ambient houses and shops.
The existing bespoke landmarks (school, hospital, library, station and the other hand-built ones) are untouched.
Style unchanged: chunky low-poly toy town, flat cheerful colours, MeshLambertMaterial, shared cached materials and geometry.
The existing builder signatures and their userData contract (animate/react hooks, sign handling) still work, so the construction sequence and landmark activities are unaffected.
No landmark newly exceeds its plot in .ai/audit-landmark-extents.mjs.
constraints: Work only in src/buildings/extras.js, src/buildings/procedural.js, src/config/landmarks.js and new files under .ai/. Do NOT modify src/world/props.js, src/world/scenery.js, src/core/materials.js, the HUD, index.html, style.css, the camera, the audio system, src/systems/pedestrians.js or src/systems/vehicles.js - other work is happening in those files concurrently and a conflicting edit will be thrown away.
You may READ src/world/props.js and src/core/materials.js and call their exports; just do not edit them.
Do not redesign the existing hand-built landmarks.
Do not add downloaded 3D models, image textures or new asset files.
Do not change lot positions, town layout or src/config/town.js.
Do not grow a building past its lot envelope.
Keep per-frame cost flat: no new per-frame CPU work, no new lights, no shadow-map changes.
validation: node .ai/audit-landmark-extents.mjs http://localhost:5199 - no NEW landmark may spill past its plot (start the dev server with: npm run dev -- --port 5199)

Capture each landmark you reworked with a Playwright script under .ai/ (model .ai/capture-target.mjs, which builds one landmark and photographs it) and check the result yourself for clipping, floating parts, bad ground contact and blank faces before reporting done
Zero page errors in the capture run
